title: Kiratpur Sahib
hookLine: many Sikhs immerse the ashes of the dead in the river here

lines: A QUIET DRIVE, A WHITE BUNDLE.
cards: Nobody in the car says much on the long drive. In someone's lap sits a small bundle wrapped in white cloth. At the end of the road there's a river, the Sutlej, running fast and gray-green past a gurdwara on its bank.

A family walks down to the water together, stands for a prayer, and lets the ashes go. The current takes them at once. This is Kiratpur Sahib, and Sikh families come here from near and far to do exactly this.

teach.b: First, the town. Kiratpur, on the Sutlej, is linked in tradition with Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, who spent his later years here: a town of the Gurus' families and memories.

Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib stands on the bank, where Sikh families bring the ashes of the people they love, say the Ardas, and place them in the flowing water. Third, what Sikh teaching says, and doesn't.

The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, says, in paraphrase, that after cremation the ashes may be put into any flowing water nearby, and it discourages building monuments over them. So no single place is required.
Kiratpur isn't a rule. It's a choice made out of love, because the Gurus' own memory is close by. Fourth, the hymn.
At night, and at the time of a funeral, Sikhs sing the Kirtan Sohila.
In it Guru Nanak pictures death as a wedding day, in paraphrase: the day of the wedding is written; come, friends, pour oil on the threshold; give me your blessings, that I may meet my Lord.
The house is full of people getting a bride ready to go.
That's how the hymn sees the last leaving: not an end, but someone going home to the beloved. So at the riverbank, a family can grieve, and still hear the wedding song. Both are allowed.

how: After a cremation, Sikh families often bring the ashes to Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib at Kiratpur, say the Ardas, and place them in the Sutlej; others use any nearby flowing water, as the Rehat Maryada allows.

games.q: a family far from Punjab wonders what to do with a grandmother's ashes. what does the Rehat Maryada say?
o: they must be carried to Kiratpur.
they may go into any flowing water nearby.
they should be kept under a monument.
games.why: any flowing water will do, and the code discourages monuments. families who choose Kiratpur do it out of love, not rule.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone you love who is far away, and let their face or their voice come without hurrying.
Picture a river moving past, steady and fast, and if you'd like, set one small memory of theirs on the water and watch the current carry it on. If you pray, remember them in your own words.
If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Kiratpur Sahib. The town on the Sutlej, linked with Guru Hargobind, where Sikh families bring the ashes of the dead to the river at Patalpuri. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: ashes to the river. Grief and the wedding song can share one riverbank. Go gently.
